newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian survivors of shipwreck return to India.
newsitem.headline: Indian survivors of shipwreck return to India.

text.p: Twenty-two illegal immigrants, survivors of a shipwreck in the Mediterranean in which around 280 of their companions drowned, arrived back in India early on Sunday.

The men, mostly in their early 20s, were among some 100 from India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka sent home by Greece after their bid for a more prosperous life in Europe came to grief in the waters between Malta and Sicily on Christmas Day.
Indian police met the deportees, who according to earlier newspaper reports were mainly from the northern state of Punjab, as they arrived at Bombay airport.
They were to be flown to New Delhi later on Sunday to gather statements for a case already being investigated by the Greek police and Interpol.

The survivors have alleged that some 300 of their companions were forced at gunpoint to transfer in choppy seas from the Honduran-flagged Yioham to a fishing boat, which then sank after the two vessels collided.
"I was in the sinking boat when my friends lowered a rope so that I could climb on to the ship," Sadnam Singh told Reuters as the police led the men away.
Only 29 people were rescued from the sinking boat, and the Yioham continued its journey to Greece, where the survivors and another 110 immigrants still on the Yiohan were arrested.
A Greek prosecutor has charged three Greek sailors -- crew members of the two ships -- with mass murder. They are all still at liberty.

Nafplion prosecutor Yannis Provataris also charged eight other people, including foreigners, with illegal movement of immigrants in Greece and said evidence "led to the conclusion there was a collision, a shipwreck, and that many people drowned".
Greek police said they had arrested two Indians and a Pakistani involved in the case but gave no further details.
Singh said his family paid more than 200,000 rupees ($5,580) to agents recruiting immigrant labourers to work in Greece and Italy.
He said he had been flown to Cairo, via Amman, and kept aboard a ship on the Egyptian coast for months before being transferred to the Yioham for the ill-fated voyage.
